title: Netflix Did Not Kill Blockbuster
author: Eddie Killian
summary: The standard disruption narrative—Netflix arrived and Blockbuster failed to adapt—is too clean to be useful. Killian argues Blockbuster died because its own model had become structurally incoherent before Netflix had enough power to finish the job: Netflix did not create the contradiction, it exposed it. The first fracture was in the receipt. Late fees were not a side feature—they were financially material ($400-450M in projected 2005 revenue)—yet they put the company in direct conflict with the customer it claimed to serve. This created a trap: keeping fees preserved revenue but eroded loyalty; removing them threatened the economics. Netflix offered not better technology but better alignment—it made the customer's desired behavior (no penalties, less friction, more choice) economically central, while Blockbuster's model rewarded the exact behavior customers wanted to avoid. The lesson transfers to any organization that monetizes customer frustration: payment is not loyalty, habit is not consent, and lack of alternatives is not satisfaction.
points: Blockbuster's model had become structurally unstable before Netflix was large enough to end it—Netflix exposed the incoherence, it didn't create it.

Late fees were financially material ($400-450M projected revenue for 2005), but they put Blockbuster in direct economic conflict with the customer it claimed to serve—a structurally dangerous position.
Revenue can become a lagging indicator of coherence: a company can still be large, familiar, and busy while the model underneath it has already lost stability.

Netflix's advantage was alignment, not technology: it made the customer's desired behavior (no fees, no trip, more choice) the engine of the business, while Blockbuster's model rewarded customer failure.

The lesson transfers to any organization that monetizes customer frustration—banks on nuisance fees, software on lock-in, hospitals on billing complexity: trapped customers are not committed customers.
quotes: Blockbuster died because its own model had become unstable before Netflix had enough power to finish the job. Netflix did not create the contradiction. Netflix exposed it.
That is a dangerous kind of business model because it puts the company in conflict with the person it claims to serve.
Revenue can become a lagging indicator of coherence. It can preserve the appearance of strength after the underlying structure has begun to fail.
Payment is not loyalty. Habit is not consent. Lack of alternatives is not satisfaction.
The most dangerous competitor is not always the one with better technology. It is the one whose model makes the customer’s desired behavior more profitable than yours can.
The company did not die because the future arrived. It died because the future audited the model, and the model failed.
